newsitem.title: UK: Former UK Chancellor says BUBA is right on gold.
newsitem.headline: Former UK Chancellor says BUBA is right on gold.

text.p: Former British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Thursday German government plans to revalue gold and currency assets to help cut its budget deficit should play no part in its push to join a single European currency.
"I'm on the side of the Bundesbank in this particular dispute," Clarke told BBC television. "No-one should go into a single currency unless the convergence criteria are genuinely met."

The Bundesbank rejected Bonn's plan to revalue assets, saying it could undermine the euro from the start. It added that the higher valuation of reserves would only be of limited help to the lasting improvement of public finances.

Clarke said one-off "accounting devices" should be ignored when judging the fitness of a nation's public finances for European economic and monetary union. The underlying state of tax, borrowing and public debt was what counted.

"You should set on one side what the French have done with Telecoms pensions, set on one side what the Italians have done with their Euro tax and set on one side what the German government wants to do revaluing gold," he said.
Earlier this year, the French government reduced its budget deficit by counting as revenue a 37 billion franc payment from state-owned France Telecom to meet future pension liabilities.
In Italy, meanwhile, the government has cut its public debt with a so-called Euro tax.
Clarke is the only Europhile of the six contenders for the leadership of the Conservative Party, so his latest comments were aimed just as much at a domestic as a European audience.

He said he had always said EMU was unlikely to start on time in January 1, 1999. "There could be advantages (to joining EMU), there could be disadvantages. There will be no advantages if countries go ahead on the basis of accounting devices. What matters is the underlying reality."

The Bundesbank would likely endorse that view. Its statement released on Wednesday said: "The negative knock-on effects on the interpretation of the entry criteria and the stability policy credibility of the selection of participants in May 1998 would scarcely be avoidable."
